title: Fortress Betio
pull: Built to stop an invasion at the water's edge

facts.text: Betio was the main Japanese stronghold in the Gilbert Islands. By November 1943 its garrison included the 3rd Special Base Force, the 7th Sasebo Special Naval Landing Force, the 111th Pioneers, and the 4th Construction Unit: naval infantry plus construction workers, about 1,200 of them Korean laborers.
Rear Admiral Keiji Shibasaki of the Imperial Japanese Navy took command in August 1943. His plan was to destroy any landing at the water's edge.
His men ringed the island with a barrier of logs and coral, wire, mines, and concrete obstacles, and built about 500 pillboxes and strongpoints covered with logs, steel, and sand.
Betio had 14 coast defense guns. The biggest were four British made Vickers 8 inch naval guns in turrets.
Shibasaki is said to have told his men that a million men could not take Tarawa in a hundred years.

On 20 November the 8 inch guns fired the opening shots of the battle at the American ships. Battleship fire knocked them out quickly, although one kept up an intermittent, inaccurate fire into the second day.
The bombardment cut the admiral's above ground telephone wires. With no backup, he could not organize the counterattack that might have thrown the Marines off their thin beachhead on the first night.

Sources disagree on when Shibasaki died. Accounts drawing on Japanese records say a shell killed him and much of his staff on the afternoon of 20 November; the 1947 Marine history says 21 November, and the 1993 Marine history says 22 November.
Of the defenders, 4,690 died. Only 17 wounded Japanese were captured, along with 129 Korean laborers.
Shibasaki's concrete command blockhouse took direct hits from 16 inch shells and 500 pound bombs and survived. It still stands on Betio.

declassified.fact: For decades the Betio guns were called the "Singapore guns", supposedly captured from the British in 1942. In 1977 the writer William H. Bartsch examined them and found Vickers markings, and company records showed they were among 12 eight inch guns sold to Japan in 1905, during the Russo Japanese War. The Japanese never captured any 8 inch guns at Singapore.
